extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, translators of classical texts, and educated general readers interested in literary criticism and translation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for translating and critically assessing classical moral/philosophical works and modern poets (e.g., Marcus Aurelius, Heine), emphasizing accessibility, fidelity of thought, style, and emotional force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat ancient works as living documents with modern applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient authors and remains (e.g., Marcus Aurelius) should be treated not as dead learning but as documents with modern applicability and living interest; their chief value lies in their side of modern applicability to present life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator/critic should present classical texts as 'food for men' engaged in contemporary life rather than as museum-pieces for schoolboys; emphasize examples and notes that connect ancient thought to current affairs and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render in plain, popular, and idiomatic language for the general public
rubrics_metrics.description: A translator's aim should be to make Marcus Aurelius (and similar authors) accessible: use perfectly plain, unprofessional language and common vocabulary so the work 'volitare per ora virum' (fly about men's mouths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer familiar words (e.g., 'pence' not 'denarii'), use the name by which the author is best known (call him 'Marcus Aurelius' rather than 'Marcus Antoninus'), and avoid formal Latinate or pedantic terms (e.g., use 'Ethics' instead of 'Ethic'). The translator should write for the general public rather than a small scholarly circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize fidelity of thought even when original language is corrupt
rubrics_metrics.description: When the original (e.g., the Greek of Marcus Aurelius) is corrupt, hard, or obscure, the translator should firmly seize upon and render the clear thought underlying the troubled wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render the meaning distinctly and, where appropriate, throw an expressive shade around it that suits the thought's tone; accuracy of thought and substantiality are as important as stylistic features of the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance accuracy with emotional force and rhythm (fidelity vs vigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation should combine substantiality, soundness, and precision with the living spirit and force of earlier vigorous versions (contrast: Long's fidelity vs Collier's impetuosity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice emotional vigor, rhythm, or impetuosity for mere literal correctness; where predecessor translations have valuable spirit, attempt to preserve that energy while improving on accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be charitable when critiquing predecessor translations
rubrics_metrics.description: A translator should deal leniently with predecessors and avoid excessively harsh, personal terms when describing earlier versions (the critic objects to calling Collier's work 'a most coarse and vulgar copy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge predecessors' virtues (e.g., spirit, vigor) even if their scholarship is imperfect; temper scholarly judgment with respect for the benefit provided to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry; prefer accessibility over punctilious accuracy of phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Small matters of phrase and nomenclature (e.g., 'Ethic' vs 'Ethics', 'Hellenes' vs 'Greeks') are important for the general public: translators should avoid pedantic forms that impede popular understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose idiomatic, simple, and familiar renderings; aim for currency and recognizability rather than technical exactness when addressing a broad audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make account of the translator's stylistic choices relative to the original's physiognomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all original languages' stylistic physiognomy is essential; e.g., Marcus Aurelius's Greek lacks the distinctive charm of Thucydides or Plato, so losing some original 'physiognomy' in translation is acceptable if the content and practical value are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether preserving the original author's linguistic personality is necessary for readers' appreciation; prioritize conveying contents that matter to modern readers over slavish mimicry of an unattractive original style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present moral or philosophical writings with practical, uplifting applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral systems and moral writings should not merely state rules; their power lies in supplying the joyful, bounding emotion that carries people to practice — religion's strength is that it 'lighted up' morality with inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating or teaching moral texts, highlight elements that inspire and vivify (emotion, practical prompts) so that rules become practicable for ordinary readers rather than abstract burdens for sages alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep emphasis on inward life and personal record when assessing moral figures
rubrics_metrics.description: For figures like Marcus Aurelius the chief interest is their inward life (Journal/Meditations) rather than external incidents; the private memoranda supply the most valuable record of moral worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical and critical accounts should foreground personal journals and inner testimonies as primary evidence of character and practical instruction, using outward anecdotes only as secondary illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain authorial voice and authenticity rather than artificial objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry and narrative (e.g., Heine's Romancero), avoidance of 'beautiful objectivity' — that is, attempting to impersonate other eras or voices — is preferable; the writer should remain himself rather than become an ancient or foreign persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the author's contemporary sensibility and voice; authenticity and the poet's own perspective often produce more vitality than forced impersonation of other historical or cultural personae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the fusion of aesthetic clarity and intense, sublime feeling in great poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: A powerful poet combines 'Greek' qualities (perfection of literary form, love of clearness and beauty) with 'Hebrew' qualities (intensity, untamableness, a 'longing which cannot be uttered') to reach the infinite goal of poetry and art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In critical judgment or creative practice, seek and praise works that unite formal beauty and clarity with depth of feeling and sublimity; assess poems on both formal perfection and emotional/ideational intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony and modern inflection skillfully, with a culminating bite
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective modern irony (as in Heine) is masterly when it pervades a passage and finishes with a grim or pointed innuendo that reveals the author's stance and modern sensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft ironical passages that build tone and then deliver a decisive concluding line or innuendo; value irony that is both subtle and sharply revealing rather than gratuitous sarcasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical tone: note faults but emphasize positive contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a great but morally or personally flawed artist (e.g., Heine), mark negative traits where necessary but avoid lingering on them; prefer to conclude by asserting the subject's positive and lasting contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After acknowledging defects (intemperance, unscrupulous attacks, sensuality), focus criticism on the artist's achievements and place in literary history; critics should balance moral censure with recognition of artistic importance.
